subject: biology

items.q: Which statement describes the cells formed by meiosis?
items.correct: They are all genetically different from each other.
items.misconception: They are all genetically identical to each other.
items.why: Both meiosis and mitosis are taught as 'cell division' and both start by making copies of the genetic information, so students merge them into one process and carry the identical-cell outcome of mitosis across to meiosis. Meiosis leads to non-identical cells being formed while mitosis leads to identical cells being formed. In sexual reproduction the mixing of genetic information leads to variety in the offspring.
items.random_wrong: There are two of them formed from the parent cell.

items.q: Which statement about sexual reproduction in a flowering plant is correct?
items.correct: In plants, pollen and egg cells fuse, mixing genetic information.
items.misconception: In plants, the gametes made by meiosis are all identical cells.
items.why: Both meiosis and mitosis are taught as 'cell division' and both start by making copies of the genetic information, so students merge them into one process and carry the identical-cell outcome of mitosis across to meiosis. Meiosis leads to non-identical cells being formed while mitosis leads to identical cells being formed. In sexual reproduction the mixing of genetic information leads to variety in the offspring.
items.random_wrong: In plants, one parent's gametes fuse without a second parent.

items.q: Which statement describes asexual reproduction?
items.correct: One parent is involved and only mitosis takes place.
items.misconception: One parent is involved and meiosis forms identical cells.
items.why: Both meiosis and mitosis are taught as 'cell division' and both start by making copies of the genetic information, so students merge them into one process and carry the identical-cell outcome of mitosis across to meiosis. Meiosis leads to non-identical cells being formed while mitosis leads to identical cells being formed. In sexual reproduction the mixing of genetic information leads to variety in the offspring.
items.random_wrong: One parent is involved and its gametes fuse together.

items.q: A cell in the reproductive organ of a mouse divides to form gametes. What is the result?
items.correct: Four cells form by meiosis, all genetically different.
items.misconception: Two cells form by meiosis, both genetically different.
items.why: Students remember that meiosis halves the chromosome number and wrongly apply the same halving to the number of cells, or they recall mitosis producing two cells and assume meiosis does the same. When a cell divides to form gametes, copies of the genetic information are made and the cell divides twice to form four gametes, each with a single set of chromosomes and all genetically different from each other.
items.random_wrong: Four cells form by mitosis, all genetically identical.

items.q: A body cell of a species contains 20 chromosomes. What happens to chromosome number during reproduction?
items.correct: Meiosis gives gametes with 10; fertilisation restores 20.
items.misconception: Meiosis gives gametes with 20; fertilisation reduces to 10.
items.why: The two processes are always described in the same sentence, and 'fertilisation' is the more memorable word, so students attach the halving to the wrong one. Meiosis halves the number of chromosomes in gametes and fertilisation restores the full number of chromosomes.
items.random_wrong: Meiosis gives two gametes with 10; fertilisation gives 20.

items.q: What happens after two gametes join at fertilisation?
items.correct: The new cell divides by mitosis and cells differentiate.
items.misconception: The new cell divides by meiosis, then cells differentiate.
items.why: Meiosis has just been met in the context of reproduction, so students attach it to every stage of reproduction rather than only to the formation of gametes. Gametes join at fertilisation to restore the normal number of chromosomes. The new cell then divides by mitosis, the number of cells increases, and as the embryo develops cells differentiate.
items.random_wrong: The new cell divides by mitosis and then forms four gametes.

items.q: A grower has one healthy strawberry plant and wants many identical plants quickly. Why is reproduction by runners an advantage here?
items.correct: One parent is needed and it is faster than sexual reproduction.
items.misconception: Two parents share the work, so less time and energy are needed here.
items.why: Students assume that two parents means the effort is halved, and they treat sexual reproduction as the 'normal' and therefore most efficient method because it is the one they know best. Advantages of asexual reproduction are that only one parent is needed, it is more time and energy efficient as there is no need to find a mate, it is faster than sexual reproduction, and many identical offspring can be produced when conditions are favourable.
items.random_wrong: The offspring produced will show useful variation from the parent.

items.q: Which statement about organisms that reproduce by both methods is correct?
items.correct: Malarial parasites reproduce sexually in the mosquito.
items.misconception: Daffodils reproduce by bulb division, fusing gametes.
items.why: Students learn that reproduction means making a new organism and associate all reproduction with gametes, so they assume the gametes must still fuse even when only one parent is involved. Asexual reproduction involves only one parent and no fusion of gametes. There is no mixing of genetic information and only mitosis is involved, which leads to genetically identical offspring (clones).
items.random_wrong: Malarial parasites reproduce only by one method, asexually.

items.q: A population of fungi lives in a habitat where conditions are beginning to change. Why may reproducing sexually be an advantage?
items.correct: It produces variation, giving a survival advantage by natural selection.
items.misconception: Asexual reproduction is what produces the variation needed in this habitat.
items.why: Students see variation between individual plants or fungi grown from the same parent and assume the differences must be genetic, rather than caused by the environment. Asexual reproduction involves no fusion of gametes and no mixing of genetic information, which leads to genetically identical offspring (clones). It is sexual reproduction that produces variation in the offspring.
items.random_wrong: It is faster and uses less energy than reproducing asexually would be.

items.q: Which statement describes the structure of DNA?
items.correct: A polymer of two strands forming a double helix
items.misconception: A chemical stored loosely in the cell's cytoplasm
items.why: Students picture the cell as a bag of contents and remember that ribosomes and other structures are in the cytoplasm, so they place the DNA there too. The genetic material in the nucleus of a cell is composed of a chemical called DNA. The DNA is contained in structures called chromosomes.
items.random_wrong: A polymer of four bases joined into two long strands

items.q: What is meant by the genome of an organism?
items.correct: The entire genetic material of an organism
items.misconception: The amino acids that make up an organism's DNA
items.why: Students learn that DNA codes for a sequence of amino acids and that both DNA and protein are polymers, so they attach the amino acid unit to the wrong molecule. DNA is a polymer made from four different nucleotides. Each nucleotide consists of a common sugar and phosphate group with one of four different bases attached to the sugar. It is the protein, not the DNA, that is a sequence of amino acids.
items.random_wrong: The parts of the DNA that code for proteins

items.q: A gene in a mouse is linked to brown fur. What does that gene code for?
items.correct: A certain sequence of amino acids
items.misconception: The brown fur characteristic directly
items.why: Everyday phrases like 'the gene for blue eyes' skip the protein step entirely, so students learn a direct gene-to-characteristic link. A gene is a small section of DNA on a chromosome, and each gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids, to make a specific protein. The alleles present operate at a molecular level to develop characteristics that can be expressed as a phenotype.
items.random_wrong: One amino acid for each single base

items.q: Which of these is one of the uses of understanding the human genome?
items.correct: Searching for genes linked to some diseases
items.misconception: Finding the gene that directly builds a feature
items.why: Everyday phrases like 'the gene for blue eyes' skip the protein step entirely, so students learn a direct gene-to-characteristic link. A gene is a small section of DNA on a chromosome, and each gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids, to make a specific protein. The alleles present operate at a molecular level to develop characteristics that can be expressed as a phenotype.
items.random_wrong: Removing non-coding DNA, which has no effect

items.q: DNA is a polymer. Which describes the repeating unit it is made from?
items.correct: A nucleotide of sugar, phosphate and one of four bases
items.misconception: An amino acid joined to a sugar and phosphate group
items.why: Students learn that DNA codes for a sequence of amino acids and that both DNA and protein are polymers, so they attach the amino acid unit to the wrong molecule. DNA is a polymer made from four different nucleotides. Each nucleotide consists of a common sugar and phosphate group with one of four different bases attached to the sugar. It is the protein, not the DNA, that is a sequence of amino acids.
items.random_wrong: A base joined directly on to the next base in the strand

items.q: A coding section of DNA contains 30 bases. How many amino acids does this code for?
items.correct: 10, because three bases code for one amino acid
items.misconception: 30, because one base codes for one amino acid
items.why: Students see the four bases lined up along the strand and match them one-to-one with the units of the protein, because a one-to-one code seems simpler. A sequence of three bases is the code for a particular amino acid, and the order of bases controls the order in which amino acids are assembled to produce a particular protein.
items.random_wrong: 15, because each pair of bases codes for one acid

items.q: What forms the two long strands of a DNA molecule?
items.correct: Alternating sugar and phosphate sections
items.misconception: Nucleotides made only of the four bases
items.why: Students only ever write out DNA as a string of letters, so the base is the only part of the unit they ever see named, and the word nucleotide becomes another name for it. DNA is a polymer made from four different nucleotides. Each nucleotide consists of a common sugar and phosphate group with one of four different bases attached to the sugar.
items.random_wrong: Four bases joined end to end in order

items.q: In the complementary strands of DNA, how are the bases linked?
items.correct: C is linked to G, and T is linked to A
items.misconception: A is linked to C, while G is linked to T
items.why: Students remember only that the bases pair up and recall the list 'A, C, G, T' in order, pairing the first with the second and the third with the fourth. In the complementary strands a C is always linked to a G on the opposite strand and a T to an A.
items.random_wrong: Every base links to the next base along

items.q: Where are proteins synthesised, and how do the amino acids reach the chain?
items.correct: On ribosomes; carrier molecules bring the amino acids
items.misconception: On ribosomes; the DNA strand itself is the amino acids
items.why: Students learn that DNA codes for a sequence of amino acids and that both DNA and protein are polymers, so they attach the amino acid unit to the wrong molecule. DNA is a polymer made from four different nucleotides. Each nucleotide consists of a common sugar and phosphate group with one of four different bases attached to the sugar. It is the protein, not the DNA, that is a sequence of amino acids.
items.random_wrong: In the cytoplasm's DNA; carrier molecules bring bases

items.q: An enzyme is able to do its job because of which feature of the protein?
items.correct: The unique shape it folds into at the end
items.misconception: The characteristic that its gene codes for
items.why: Everyday phrases like 'the gene for blue eyes' skip the protein step entirely, so students learn a direct gene-to-characteristic link. A gene is a small section of DNA on a chromosome, and each gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids, to make a specific protein. The alleles present operate at a molecular level to develop characteristics that can be expressed as a phenotype.
items.random_wrong: The number of amino acids in its finished chain

items.q: Which statement about mutations is correct?
items.correct: Most do not alter the protein produced.
items.misconception: Each one alters the protein that is made.
items.why: Mutations are met mainly through examples of inherited disorders, so students only ever see the rare mutations that do have an effect. Mutations occur continuously. Most do not alter the protein, or only alter it slightly so that its appearance or function is not changed. A few mutations code for an altered protein with a different shape.
items.random_wrong: Only those in non-coding DNA have no effect.

items.q: A mutation changes the shape of an enzyme. What is the likely effect?
items.correct: The enzyme may no longer fit the substrate binding site.
items.misconception: Every other protein in the cell is altered in the same way.
items.why: Mutations are met mainly through examples of inherited disorders, so students only ever see the rare mutations that do have an effect. Mutations occur continuously. Most do not alter the protein, or only alter it slightly so that its appearance or function is not changed. A few mutations code for an altered protein with a different shape.
items.random_wrong: There is no effect, because this DNA is non-coding DNA.

items.q: A genetic variant is found in a non-coding part of DNA. How may it influence the phenotype?
items.correct: By altering how genes are switched on and off
items.misconception: It has no way of influencing the phenotype at all
items.why: The label 'non-coding' sounds like 'does nothing', and students have been taught that characteristics come from proteins, so DNA that makes no protein seems irrelevant. Not all parts of DNA code for proteins. Non-coding parts of DNA can switch genes on and off, so variations in these areas of DNA may affect how genes are expressed.
items.random_wrong: By coding directly for a new characteristic

items.q: A mouse has two different alleles for fur colour. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: It is heterozygous, so the dominant allele is shown.
items.misconception: It is homozygous, because two alleles are present here.
items.why: The two long words homozygous and heterozygous look similar and are learned as a pair, so students match the definitions to the wrong terms. If the two alleles present are the same the organism is homozygous for that trait, but if the alleles are different they are heterozygous.
items.random_wrong: It is heterozygous, so the recessive allele is expressed.

items.q: A plant has the genotype Tt, where T is the dominant allele. What is its phenotype?
items.correct: It shows the characteristic of the T allele.
items.misconception: It shows T only if T is common in the population.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'dominant' is 'most widespread' or 'strongest', and students transfer that meaning to the genetic term. A dominant allele is always expressed, even if only one copy is present. A recessive allele is only expressed if two copies are present.
items.random_wrong: It shows the characteristic of the t allele only.

items.q: Two heterozygous mice (Bb) are crossed, where B is dominant. Which ratio of phenotypes does a Punnett square predict?
items.correct: 3 with the dominant characteristic to 1 without
items.misconception: 1 with the dominant characteristic to 3 without
items.why: Students reason that if an allele is in the genotype it must show up in the phenotype, because they think of the genotype as a list of visible features. A recessive allele is only expressed if two copies are present (therefore no dominant allele present).
items.random_wrong: 4 with the dominant characteristic to 0 without

items.q: In a family tree, two parents who do not have cystic fibrosis have a child who does. What does this show?
items.correct: Each parent carries one recessive allele.
items.misconception: The allele causing the disorder is dominant.
items.why: Students assume that a serious disorder must be caused by a 'stronger' dominant allele and that a rarer, less harmful condition must be recessive, so they swap the two. Polydactyly (having extra fingers or toes) is caused by a dominant allele. Cystic fibrosis (a disorder of cell membranes) is caused by a recessive allele.
items.random_wrong: The parents' genotype matches their phenotype.

items.q: A student uses a single gene cross to predict a person's height. Why is this prediction unreliable?
items.correct: Most characteristics result from multiple genes interacting.
items.misconception: Every characteristic is controlled by one single gene here.
items.why: Genetic crosses and Punnett squares are always taught using single gene examples such as fur colour in mice, so students generalise that pattern to all characteristics. Some characteristics are controlled by a single gene, such as fur colour in mice and red-green colour blindness in humans, but most characteristics are a result of multiple genes interacting.
items.random_wrong: A gene codes directly for the characteristic, not protein.

items.q: In mice, black fur (B) is dominant to brown (b). A black mouse is crossed with a brown mouse and some brown offspring are produced. What was the black parent's genotype?
items.correct: Bb, since it passed on a b allele
items.misconception: BB, since its two alleles are the same
items.why: The two long words homozygous and heterozygous look similar and are learned as a pair, so students match the definitions to the wrong terms. If the two alleles present are the same the organism is homozygous for that trait, but if the alleles are different they are heterozygous.
items.random_wrong: bb, since a b allele was expressed here

items.q: Which alleles cause polydactyly and cystic fibrosis?
items.correct: Polydactyly dominant; cystic fibrosis recessive
items.misconception: Both are dominant, as the disorders are common
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'dominant' is 'most widespread' or 'strongest', and students transfer that meaning to the genetic term. A dominant allele is always expressed, even if only one copy is present. A recessive allele is only expressed if two copies are present.
items.random_wrong: Both are recessive, as one copy is enough here

items.q: A couple are offered embryo screening. Which of these is an ethical issue they might consider?
items.correct: Whether rejecting an embryo with an allele is right
items.misconception: Whether one gene controls all the embryo's traits
items.why: Genetic crosses and Punnett squares are always taught using single gene examples such as fur colour in mice, so students generalise that pattern to all characteristics. Some characteristics are controlled by a single gene, such as fur colour in mice and red-green colour blindness in humans, but most characteristics are a result of multiple genes interacting.
items.random_wrong: Whether the screening test is medically accurate

items.q: What do ordinary human body cells contain?
items.correct: 23 pairs of chromosomes, one pair determining sex
items.misconception: 23 chromosomes in total, one of them determining sex
items.why: The number 23 is the one students remember from the phrase '23 pairs', and they drop the word 'pairs' when recalling it. Ordinary human body cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes. 22 pairs control characteristics only, but one of the pairs carries the genes that determine sex.
items.random_wrong: 23 pairs of chromosomes, with XY in every female

items.q: A genetic cross is carried out between XX and XY parents. What does it predict about the offspring?
items.correct: 1 female to 1 male, so a 50% chance of each
items.misconception: Exactly 2 girls and 2 boys in four babies
items.why: A Punnett square has exactly four boxes, so students read the four boxes as four actual offspring rather than as four equally likely outcomes. A Punnett square diagram is used to make predictions using the theory of probability. The outcome of a genetic cross is expressed using direct proportion and simple ratios as a prediction, not as a guaranteed count of offspring.
items.random_wrong: All female, as the egg cell decides sex

items.q: How many sets of chromosomes does a gamete contain?
items.correct: One. Meiosis halves the number of chromosomes, so each gamete has a single set of chromosomes.
items.misconception: A gamete contains the full number of chromosomes, the same as an ordinary body cell.
items.why: Students know that copies of the genetic information are made at the start of the division, so they assume every cell produced ends up with a complete set. Meiosis halves the number of chromosomes in gametes: the cell divides twice to form four gametes, each with a single set of chromosomes. Fertilisation then restores the full number of chromosomes.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can one species reproduce both sexually and asexually?
items.correct: Yes. Some organisms reproduce by both methods depending on the circumstances, such as malarial parasites, many fungi and many plants.
items.misconception: Each species reproduces by one method only, either sexually or asexually.
items.why: Sexual and asexual reproduction are taught as a pair of opposites and compared in tables, so students treat them as two exclusive categories that organisms are sorted into. Some organisms reproduce by both methods depending on the circumstances: malarial parasites reproduce asexually in the human host but sexually in the mosquito; many fungi reproduce asexually by spores but also sexually to give variation; many plants produce seeds sexually but also reproduce asexually by runners or bulb division.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a gene the same thing as a chromosome?
items.correct: No. A gene is a small section of DNA on a chromosome, so a chromosome carries many genes.
items.misconception: A gene and a chromosome are the same structure under two different names.
items.why: The words gene, chromosome and DNA are used in the same sentences and diagrams without a clear sense of scale, so students treat them as interchangeable labels. The DNA is contained in structures called chromosomes, and a gene is a small section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a particular sequence of amino acids.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does the genome of an organism include?
items.correct: The entire genetic material of that organism, not only the parts that code for proteins.
items.misconception: The genome is just the collection of genes that code for proteins.
items.why: The word genome sounds like a plural of gene, so students read it as 'all the genes' and leave out the rest of the genetic material. The genome of an organism is the entire genetic material of that organism. Not all parts of DNA code for proteins.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What forms the long strands of a DNA molecule?
items.correct: Alternating sugar and phosphate sections, with one of the four bases attached to each sugar.
items.misconception: The four bases join end to end to form the two long strands of DNA.
items.why: Diagrams draw attention to the lettered bases in the middle of the molecule, and students read the sequence of letters as though it were the strand itself. The long strands of DNA consist of alternating sugar and phosphate sections. Attached to each sugar is one of the four bases.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where in the cell are proteins synthesised?
items.correct: On ribosomes, according to a template.
items.misconception: Proteins are synthesised in the nucleus, where the DNA is.
items.why: Students know the genetic material is in the nucleus and assume the protein must be built in the same place as the instructions are stored. Proteins are synthesised on ribosomes, according to a template. Carrier molecules bring specific amino acids to add to the growing protein chain in the correct order.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What allows a protein to do its job?
items.correct: Its unique shape. When the protein chain is complete it folds up to form a unique shape that enables it to work as an enzyme, hormone or structure such as collagen.
items.misconception: A protein's job is decided by how many amino acids it contains, not by its folded shape.
items.why: Students focus on the order of bases coding for a chain of amino acids and stop at the chain, never picturing the folding step that follows. When the protein chain is complete it folds up to form a unique shape. This unique shape enables the proteins to do their job as enzymes, hormones or forming structures in the body such as collagen.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are the genotype and the phenotype the same thing?
items.correct: No. The genotype is the alleles present; the phenotype is the characteristic that those alleles develop.
items.misconception: The genotype and the phenotype are two words for the same thing.
items.why: The two terms are introduced together, sound alike, and are often written side by side in the same table row, so students do not separate the alleles from the characteristic they produce. The alleles present, or genotype, operate at a molecular level to develop characteristics that can be expressed as a phenotype.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which parent's gamete determines the sex of a child?
items.correct: The father's. The mother's egg cells all carry an X chromosome, while sperm cells carry either an X or a Y.
items.misconception: The mother's egg cell determines the sex of the child.
items.why: Pregnancy is associated entirely with the mother, so students assume she must control every feature of the developing embryo, including its sex. In females the sex chromosomes are the same (XX) and in males they are different (XY). A genetic cross between XX and XY shows that the gamete carrying either an X or a Y determines the sex of the offspring.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which division do cells in the reproductive organs use to form gametes?
items.correct: Meiosis. Cells in the reproductive organs divide by meiosis to form gametes.
items.misconception: Gametes are formed by mitosis in the reproductive organs.
items.why: Mitosis is the division students meet first and use for all growth and repair, so they apply it as the default division for making any new cell. Cells in reproductive organs divide by meiosis to form gametes, and all gametes are genetically different from each other.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What kinds of issues does embryo screening raise?
items.correct: Economic, social and ethical issues, about which informed judgements should be made.
items.misconception: Embryo screening raises only medical issues, because it is a medical procedure.
items.why: Screening is presented in a health context, so students judge it purely by whether it works, without considering its cost, its effect on society or the ethical questions it raises. Students should make informed judgements about the economic, social and ethical issues concerning embryo screening, given appropriate information.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which sex chromosomes are found in females and which in males?
items.correct: In females the sex chromosomes are the same (XX); in males they are different (XY).
items.misconception: In females the sex chromosomes are XY and in males they are XX.
items.why: Students remember only that one sex has two different chromosomes but not which, and the letters are easy to swap when they are recalled without the XX and XY labels attached. 22 pairs control characteristics only, but one of the pairs carries the genes that determine sex. In females the sex chromosomes are the same (XX); in males the chromosomes are different (XY).
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Biology (8461) specification; section 4.6.1 Reproduction
